html:
Nisa is the ruin of a royal fortress of the Parthian Empire near Ashgabat in Turkmenistan. It was one of the first seats of the Parthian kings, from about the 3rd century BCE.

The Parthians were a people of the steppe edge who took over Iran after Alexander's heirs, and ruled from Mesopotamia to the Indus until 224 CE. At Nisa, called Mithradatkirt, they built halls and a royal treasury. Soviet diggers found carved ivory drinking horns there in Greek style, and thousands of pottery pieces with notes on wine deliveries in Parthian writing.

The finds show a mix of Greek, Iranian and steppe art. The site is a World Heritage Site and, like Merv, a source of pride for modern Turkmenistan.
